opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the original problem RLHF was trying to address is that when you pretrain a large language model, you're essentially training it to imitate the distribution of text on the internet. That gives you an enormously capable model in some sense, it's absorbed a huge amount of knowledge, but it isn't necessarily doing what you actually want. If you ask it a question, it might continue your question with more questions, or produce something plausible-sounding but unhelpful, or say something toxic, because all of those things exist in the training data. There's a gap between "likely text" and "good text."

The difficulty is that "good" is very hard to write down as an explicit objective. You can't easily specify a loss function for helpfulness, or honesty, or appropriate tone. But it turns out that humans are pretty good at looking at two responses and saying which one they prefer. So the core idea of RLHF is to use those comparative judgments to learn a reward model, essentially a learned function that scores outputs according to what people prefer, and then optimize the language model against that reward using reinforcement learning.

So in a sense, RLHF is a way of turning fuzzy human preferences into a training signal. It's an alignment tool: steering a model that already has a lot of capability toward behaviors that people actually find useful and safe.

What's interesting, and something I've been thinking about a lot, is that the reward model you learn is really a kind of energy function or verifier over outputs. It tells you how compatible a given response is with what you want. And once you view it that way, you start to ask whether the standard pipeline, where you use that signal only during training to fine-tune a policy, is the only or best way to use it. You could also use that kind of learned evaluator at inference time, to search over or iteratively refine candidate answers. That connects to a broader view I have that a lot of reasoning and generalization comes from having models that can evaluate and improve solutions, not just produce them in one shot.

r001.rationale: The response describes optimizing a model with human-preference rewards, but does not say agents exploit environmental rewards instead of completing the intended task.

r002.rationale: It frames RLHF as addressing unwanted or unsafe model behavior and using human preference judgments to steer models toward useful, safe behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it, the original problem was really an alignment problem in the most literal sense. You have these language models trained on enormous amounts of internet text, and what they learn to do is predict the next token. That's a really powerful objective, but it's not the objective we actually care about. We don't want a model that continues text the way the internet would continue it. We want a model that does what a person asks, in the way a helpful person would do it.

And the gap between those two things turned out to be pretty large. If you prompted an early GPT-3 style model with a question, it might answer, or it might generate three more questions, or it might produce something that looks like a forum thread. The knowledge was in there, but the behavior wasn't shaped toward being useful.

So the question becomes, how do you specify what you want? And this is where it gets hard, because for most of the things we care about, you can't write down a reward function. There's no formula for "this is a helpful, honest answer." But people can recognize it. If you show someone two responses, they can usually tell you which one is better, even if they couldn't have written the rule.

RLHF was essentially a clever way to exploit that asymmetry. You collect comparisons from people, you train a reward model to imitate those preferences, and then you optimize the language model against that learned reward. So you're replacing a reward you can't write down with one you can learn from human judgment.

What I find interesting, coming at it from the generative modeling side, is that this is really a question about how you compose a prior with a constraint. The pretrained model is this incredibly rich prior over language, and human feedback is a relatively small, relatively noisy signal about what we actually value. RLHF is one specific way to combine them. And I think a lot of the open questions now are about whether that's the right way, whether the reward model generalizes, whether you can over-optimize against it, and whether there are more principled ways to steer these models that don't require squeezing everything through a scalar reward.

r001.rationale: The response describes a mismatch between next-token prediction and helpful behavior, but does not say agents exploit environment rewards instead of completing the intended task.

r002.rationale: It frames RLHF’s original purpose as aligning model behavior with what people want, and explains that human comparisons help shape behavior toward useful responses.

astra-6.text:
I think the original motivation was that predicting the next token isn’t quite the same as doing what a person wants. You can train a language model on a lot of text, and it gets very good at modeling that text, but that doesn’t necessarily mean its responses will be helpful or follow your instructions.

And it’s difficult to write down a reward function that captures what makes a good answer. But people can often look at two answers and say, “I prefer this one.” So reinforcement learning with human feedback gives you a way to use those comparisons: you train a reward model to predict human preferences, then optimize the language model against that reward. The idea is to bridge the gap between being good at predicting text and producing responses that people actually want.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the gap between predicting text and giving helpful answers, but does not say agents exploit rewards instead of accomplishing the intended task.

r002.rationale: It describes RLHF’s original motivation as making responses helpful and instruction-following, using human preference comparisons to guide the model toward what people want.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the original motivation was that it’s very hard to specify exactly what we want a model to do. If you’re training a language model to predict the next word, that gives you a model that can generate plausible text, but it doesn’t necessarily give you a model that’s helpful or follows your instructions. And writing down a reward function for something like helpfulness is difficult.

But people can often look at two responses and say, “I prefer this one.” So reinforcement learning with human feedback tries to turn those judgments into a training signal. You learn a reward model from human preferences, and then optimize the language model against that reward. The idea is to bridge the gap between predicting text and producing behavior that people actually want.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the difficulty of specifying helpfulness, but does not say agents can exploit rewards instead of doing the intended task.

r002.rationale: It presents human preferences as a way to train for desired behavior, but does not identify preventing unintended behavior as an original aim of RLHF.
